APPROVAL OF ACTION OF GOVERNMENT IN SUPPORTING PRICE OF URANIUM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Whereas in the early 1970's the United States government saw fit to close its borders to foreign uranium; and whereas other producing countries, including Canada, could no longer compete for that large market; and whereas it was in the national interest of Canada to maintain a uranium industry for the ongoing health of communities such as Elliot Lake; and whereas United States companies continued to compete aggressively in other world markets during this period; and whereas the Canadian government was a member of a producers group which maintained a base export price; and whereas a committee of the U.S. Congress has, over Canadian objections, released confidential Canadian government documents and is thereby determining what is in the Canadian public interest, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac):
That this House support the action the Canadian government took in belonging to a producers group which was necessary for the economic survival of the Canadian uranium industry and that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should make a strong official protest to the American government in this matter of extra territorial application of American law in Canada.

subsubtopic: BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE-MINISTER'S STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall now make a statement on all circumstances regarding and surrounding the matter popularly known as the APLQ affair in Montreal, as requested by members of the House. 1 shall try to the best of my knowledge and ability to state all related facts.
As we all know, Mr. Speaker, the court proceedings initiated by the Minister of Justice of Quebec, after the illegal search of the premises occupied by l'Agence de Presse Libre du Quebec, le Mouvement pour la defense des prisonniers politiques du Quebec and la Cooperative des demenageurs du 1" mai, in October 1972, have now been completed. This illegal search has raised a number of questions in the minds of many people. Questions have been asked, particularly in the House, as to whether the Solicitor General of the time had approved of the search prior to its taking place and, if not, at what point in time this search was brought to his attention or that of his successor and whether appropriate action was taken at that time. Many questions also have been raised about the role of the RCMP Security Service in this matter and about its methods of operation. These questions are legitimate and require clear answers. This is what I propose to do today.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I cannot stress too highly that in a democratic society like ours, the rule of law is and must be paramount. It is the vital force without which our basic liberties run the risk of becoming empty slogans. No threat to such liberties can justify, in any way, and even with the best of intentions, the use of illegal means to protect these basic rights. Clearly, there can be no compromise in this regard; it is upon this premise that the integrity and survival of our democratic institutions and our fundamental liberties are based. If the law is not adequate to handle such dangers as threaten our liberties and our institutions, then the answer does not lie in breaking the law, but rather in changing it.

During the night of October 6-7, 1972, police officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, acting together with officers of the Surete du Quebec and la Police de Montreal, carried out a search of the premises occupied by L'Agence de Presse libre du Quebec, le Mouvement pour la defense des prisonniers politiques du Quebec and la Co-operative des Demenageurs du lcr mai. Documents were seized on the premises. The carrying out of this search had not received prior authorization by the court and, therefore, was illegal.
On May 26 of this year, the three officers of the RCMP, Surete du Quebec and la Police de Montreal, respectively, who had authorized this operation, entered a plea of guilty to a charge brought against them under section 115 of the Criminal Code by the authorities of the province of Quebec for

June 17, 1977
Royal Canadian Mounted Police
having neglected to obtain a search warrant in connection with the incident that took place on October 6-7, 1972. The police offiers were yesterday granted an absolute discharge by the court.
Neither the RCMP headquarters in Ottawa, nor the commanding officer of C Division in Montreal, nor the solicitor general at the time, the present Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), had been told of the search and seizure of documents on the premises occupied by the APLQ prior to the operation being carried out.

subsubtopic: BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE-MINISTER'S STATEMENT
speechtext: That sounds like Nixon.

subsubtopic: BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE-MINISTER'S STATEMENT
speechtext:
I do not think Nixon made any statements in the House like we are. The conversations which I have had personally with the present Minister of Supply and Services, the then commissioner of the RCMP, Mr. W. L. Higgitt, and the then director general of the security service, Mr. John Starnes, and the examination of relevant files clearly support these facts. It was only on October 10, 1972, four days later, that C Division of the RCMP in Montreal informed the RCMP headquarters in Ottawa of the search and seizure on the premises of the APLQ.
Following the search and seizure of the documents, the groups affected by these events sent telegrams or letters to a number of people. Thus, on Monday, October 9, 1972, only a few hours after the incident, the APLQ sent a telegram to the assistant commissioner of the RCMP in Montreal, to the director of la Police de Montreal and to the director of the Surete du Quebec, inquiring if their respective organizations had been responsible for the theft of documents. This telegram asked for an immediate reply. The RCMP did not provide a response to it.
(Translation]
On Monday, October 9, 1972, the three groups which had been the subject of the search and seizure, inquired, through letters sent to the Minister of Justice of Quebec and to the Solicitor General of Canada, if the RCMP, the Surete du Quebec and the Montreal police were involved in the break-in into their premises and the theft of documents. This registered letter, to which was attached a copy of the telegram addressed to the Assistant Commissioner of the RCMP in Montreal, requested that a reply be given before 11 a.m., Friday, October 13, 1972.
On Thursday, October 12, 1972, the Minister of Justice of Quebec, the Hon. Jerome Choquette, stated publicly that he had been informed that none of the three police forces, the RCMP, the Surete du Quebec and the Montreal police, had been involved in the break-in and the theft of documents on the premises occupied by the APLQ during the night of 6/7 October, 1972, adding that the appropriate authorities, namely the Montreal police, were investigating the matter. There is nothing in our files to indicate that the Quebec provincial authorities had communicated with the RCMP in Ottawa, or the Solicitor General of Canada or his office, before Mr. Choquette made his statement.

On Friday, October 13, 1972, spokesmen for the three groups that had written to the Solicitor General of Canada and to the Minister of Justice of Quebec held a press conference, during which they indicated they had come to the conclusion that the theft of documents was the result of a police search under the provincial Law 51. These groups took the opportunity to launch an opposition campaign against Law 51, which granted special powers of search to the police, under the control of the Police Commission of Quebec, in the fight against organized crime, terrorism and subversion.
Concerning the letter sent to the Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer, it was received in the Ministry of the Solicitor General on October 11, 1972, and brought to the attention of the RCMP by the assistant to the minister, Lieutenant Colonel John R. Cameron, in order that a reply could be prepared for the Solicitor General's signature. This was done without the minister being informed. In referring the letter directly to the RCMP for reply, without bringing it to the minister's personal attention first, Lieutenant Colonel Cameron was following the usual practice in handling such letters, addressed to the Solicitor General of Canada. This practice was meant to enable the RCMP to launch an investigation forthwith even if it meant that the letter of inquiry would be brought to the minister's attention at a later date. In fact, letters are, from time to time, addressed to the Solicitor General enquiring or complaining about the conduct of the RCMP or of one of its members in the performance of their duties as the national police force or as provincial police under arrangements that exist in eight Canadian provinces, hence the need for such a system. On October 26, 1972, the RCMP wrote to the minister's assistant, recommending that no acknowledgement be made, without providing the reason for their recommendation.
The Solicitor General of the time remembers having seen the letter of October 9, 1972, at a later date, and having asked the RCMP why they recommended that there be no acknowledgement. The Solicitor General recalls that the RCMP response to his question was that the theft of documents, about which the APLQ had complained, fell under the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities, more particularly, the Minister of Justice of Quebec, and that the Montreal police was investigating the incident. Moreover, the minister considered it hard to believe that the RCMP would have participated in a theft of documents, as the letter of October 9, 1972, had implied. It would seem, from the agenda of the minister, that the letter would have been discussed with the RCMP on November 6, 1972, just a few days after the federal general election of October 30, 1972. It is at this point that the minister would personally have seen the letter for the first time.

speechtext:
The House resumed from Thursday, June 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens:
That the Anti-Inflation Act being chapter 75, Statutes of Canada 1974-75-76, as amended by chapter 98, Statutes of Canada 1974-75-76, shall expire on the 30th day of June, 1977.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS OF JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for a few minutes this afternoon I want to address my remarks to the motion brought by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) which was debated yesterday. I think certain things ought to be said bluntly on this second day of debate. The first is that we on this side are getting a little tired of suggestions that we do not have a position on the economic problems of the country, and that we do not have a position on what should, or should not, be done with respect to controls. The fact is, we have had a position on controls and the economic difficulties of this country for a long time. Not only that, but if the positions we have taken, going back some three or four years, had been accepted by the House at the time, we would not have anything like the difficulties we face today.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS OF JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS OF JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext:
1 want to add something to that, Mr. Speaker. The fact of the matter is that under our former leader, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), this party had the guts to tell the Canadian people what no other party in this House had the guts to tell them. We were the first to suggest that something had to be done to break inflation expectations, and if it had been done at the time we were saying it we would have finished with controls a long time ago.
1 have said in this House before, and apparently I have to say it again, that there was nothing in recent history more deliberately dishonest than the 1974 election campaign of the government when they had their own contingency plan for controls and yet went through the election campaign leaving the impression, especially with labour, that they would not bring in a controls system. We put forward these ideas in 1973 and campaigned in 1974 knowing perfectly well that we did not have all segments of public opinion on our side. We knew we were in a battle against public opinion, but we were prepared to fight that battle because it was time politicians had the guts to put their ideas forward and persuade the public to adopt them-not just wait to see in what way the public would go.

In defence of the fact that he cannot find a way, if he wants to get out of controls, stay in controls for a long time, or stay in controls permanently, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) said, in effect, last night, "You cannot assail me. The polls in Canada show that the public does not want to get out of controls." I interjected, "What are you doing, making economic decisions by taking polls of what people think they like or do not like?"
The public is sick and tired of a government and of politicians who have forgotten the one fundamental obligation of a politician in Canada, and that is to decide what is the right thing to do and then persuade the public to go along with it: not the opposite. As I said, I am fed up listening to hon. members on the other side, from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance, down through the treasury benches, asking what we would do. I can see them sitting there twisting their limp wrists and saying, "Tell us what you would do." We told them many months ago, and we are telling them again.
Hon. members are smiling, but maybe that is the last thing they have to smile about. Now they are in the crunch. If they do not want to accept our point of view, they should say so. But they should go one step further and tell us what they are going to do. For 20 months this government has not known what to do. First of all, they got into this program on the wrong foot. Second, instead of starting with a freeze which would have affected everybody equally, they started with utter confusion. Third, they have not decided things amongst themselves. Now they wonder why they have problems with labour in this country: labour thinks the government has double-crossed them. We can tell the government what we would do. They should not accuse us of having no ideas. We know what we would do, and we have put it clearly to them. It is up to the government to respond; that is what this debate is all about.
This party has done a service to the country by bringing this motion forward, because the country does not know what the government has in mind in terms of a decontrols period. In all sincerity I ask the government not to leave the country in doubt very much longer. It is doubt and uncertainty that is causing as much trouble now as the inflationary expectations caused a couple of years ago. I do not have to remind anybody in this House that there are about one million people unemployed in this country. The government certainly knows that. Many members on that side understand, as we do, that the problem of unemployment will only be solved if we get the economy going, get productivity going and create a climate for the private sector in which it can do some planning and accumulate plant and equipment. It cannot do that until it knows what the government's plans are.
That being the case, I say there is a direct, blunt, real and urgent obligation on the government to tell the House today
June 17, 1977

what they are going to do. I do not want to hear any more talk from the government side-or from the media-to the effect that we cannot ask the government what they will do unless we have a plan ourselves. Mr. Speaker, we have offered a blueprint already, but the government does not want to accept it, according to the speech made by the Minister of Finance last night. The Minister of Finance said nothing.

It does not tell this country's business community where the government wants to go, does not tell labour, our working men and women, where the government intends to go, and does not tell old age pensioners, people on fixed incomes, people outside the trade union movement, ordinary entrepreneurs and small businessmen, what the government intends to do. subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS OF JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext:
What does it mean for the country? It means this: the longer the government delays making up its own mind, making a decision, the longer the country will be left in uncertainty.
Last night the hon. member for Halifax, my former leader, made a fine speech in which he quoted the Prime Minister as saying that it is the duty of the government to decide. The Prime Minister was not the first politician to say it, but it is signicant that he, this country's most prominent politician, does not abide by those words, because the government has not decided. It is one thing to say these things, quite another to act.
I have been interested to note that for some months colleagues in this House, honourable men and women all of them, have read into the record columns printed in the press, and quoted especially the results of seminars and gatherings of this country's business and labour people; and it is apparent that those who have a direct interest in the economy are unable to make up their minds on what to do. I do not say these decisions are easy; I do not pretend they are, even though I castigated the government. However, my castigation will be to some purpose if the government listens. My point is this: we must find a way out, but the final decision under our parliamentary system must be made by the government. You see, it is curious-I suppose it is one of the peccadilloes of human nature-that when we advocated controls in 1973 and 1974, people opposed us, saying we should not do it. It is somewhat ironic that today some of those very people say, "We do not want controls, but for goodness sake do not get out of them now."
Anti-Inflation Act
There is no good time for removing controls, but this may be the best opportunity we shall have for a long time. As others have said, our production is at 80 per cent of potential, one million are unemployed, but many forces at work in the economy militate against another wage and price explosion. On page 2 of the government document "Highlights of the Discussion Paper on Decontrol and Post-Control Issues" the following words appear:
The time is approaching to remove the temporary control over prices and incomes, and there are favourable conditions for doing so. It seems unlikely that excess demand will lead to a renewed acceleration of inflation when controls are removed. There should be no shortages of food, industrial materials or energy. Controls do not seem to have distorted Canadian labour or product markets, or wage or price structures.
I am not sure I agree with that last sentence. I continue quoting:
Most important, inflationary expectations have changed significantly since October 1975. Canadians no longer expect wages and prices to rise at doubledigit rates. Business and consumers do not foresee substantial price increases.
Ironically, the document says that in other areas there may be pressures on prices, possibly causing them to rise. I say to hon. members on the government side, these words are contained in the government's own document. You know, it is getting late in the day to have it both ways.

speechtext: Not if you are Liberal.

I say to the government, you had better act on this document, or tell us why you will not act.
I now come to an important point which all Canadians must face. I know the Minister of Finance would like to end controls; I know it, not because he sent me a letter, but from paying attention to what he has said. He repeated this sentiment again in last night's speech. I happen to know that a good many members on the government side would like controls to end, and I also know that a good many on the government side, although not all of them, think that longterm or permanent controls will do this country a lot of harm. That is my party's position, and it is the view of most people who are prepared to accept the responsibilities and risks which go with a free system. But the Prime Minister has said we must not get out of controls until we have a commitment from various sectors of the economy that they will restrain their demands, that demands will not get out of hand. It is fine to say that in the classroom. That is great in theory. The trouble is, the world does not work that way. It is like saying to Canadians, "We are not going to give you the freedom to make mistakes until we are absolutely sure you will not make a mistake." Such thinking applies to a world which does not exist.
This country is made up of men and women brought up in the tradition that our institutions are free. And they are free to make mistakes. Surely the government need only intervene when those mistakes are so serious as to hurt the welfare of the entire community, that is to say, when they are clearly against the public interest. My friends opposite may say, "You are being philosophical." Perhaps it is a philosophical point. The fundamental question is, are we to be a free country, or is the

June 17, 1977
Anti-Inflation Act
government to intrude on our freedoms by insisting that the state has the right to intrude in every facet of our lives?

speechtext: That is what they want.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS OF JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext: You see, it does not do for businessmen to say, "We do not think we should have controls, but if you get out of them those trade union fellows will get out of line." Do they want to return to conditions where the government does not make decisions for them, where they will have to exercise responsibility and common sense?

The more you shelter people, taking away from them the responsibility to exercise their rights within some kind of sense of self-discipline and common sense, the harder it will be for them to do it when you move them back into a free atmosphere. I say to my friends on the government side that they have not done it yet. They have not done it if they are trying to have heaven this side of the grave. However, we cannot do that. What I am saying is that there will be no perfect time to say to people that they have to be responsible, that if they want their freedom they will have to exercise it responsibly. There will be excesses. Some people will not be able to accept that. However, that is something we will have to work out as time goes on. There is not a person here with any maturity who thinks he or she lives in a perfect world or thinks he or she will ever accomplish it.
One of the things we have fought for in our community, both politically and economically, is a reasonable degree of

freedom. That results in having to be responsible. There are labour leaders today who can tell you that when controls come off the thing they fear the most is the first management group in a major sector in industry that gives way to a ridiculous demand. That will put terrible pressure on the rest of the labour leaders. They may not tell you that publicly, but they will say it privately. That means management has a responsibility. Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), last night, and reviewed his comments, along with those of others, in Hansard

June 17, 1977
Anti-Inflation Act
this morning. He has already examined the state of the economy in the context of the anti-inflation program and dealt with some of the important matters relating to the decontrol process. I assure the House that I concur with his assessment and the conclusions he drew in his review, as well as the caution that he expressed as we view decontrol and the postcontrols period.
Nobody would claim that we are out of the inflation woods yet, but I believe that we are making progress and that there are encouraging signs. The Minister of Finance mentioned some last night. I want to deal with others which directly affect my portfolio because I think they do demonstrate in a tangible way that the government has been providing leadership in the conduct of its own operations during this somewhat difficult time. I might add, Mr. Speaker, that we are fully determined to continue to provide that leadership in the equally difficult days ahead.
Let me try to review some of these encouraging signs, Mr. Speaker. The percentage increase in government spending this year is the smallest in more than a decade. I have already given a commitment to the House, which is backed up by cabinet, that fiscal restraint will continue in fiscal year 19781979. The increase in public service man years, the growth of the public service, which has been of some concern both substantively and symbolically, has been virtually halted this year, and again I have given the commitment to this House that that rigid control of manpower resources is going to continue in 1978-79.
Wage settlements negotiated with the public service unions have remained in the main in keeping with the Anti-Inflation Board guidelines. Again I can make a commitment to members of the House that, within the framework of comparability with the private sector, we will continue to offer fair but measured settlements with the federal public service, settlements that will follow and not lead the private sector.
So to the skeptics, Mr. Speaker, I would say look at the record. We were challenged to show leadership in the area of restraint and we accepted that challenge. Indeed we have met it with more than a modest measure of success. What is more, Mr. Speaker, this was accomplished without an economic distortion in the federal realm which would trigger a reaction to bounce back as soon as the controls are removed.
Therefore I think these accomplishments, together with the commitment to continue to be vigilant at the federal level in fiscal affairs, have paved the way, if and when the decision is taken, for relaxing the legislated price and income controls as they apply to federal government activity. But having said that, Mr. Speaker, I want to reiterate the caution that applies equally to the federal government as it does to all other segments of society.
We will continue to hold the upper hand with inflation only through a high level of co-operation between management and labour, between producer and manufacturer, and between government and the private sector. It is this continuing need that makes the concept of a forum for consultation as proposed in the green paper, which seems to be coming under some fire,

so attractive. We simply have to face the fact that governments cannot do it all; we will have to continue to work together. Let us make no mistake about it; the road ahead will not be as easy, nor can the controls period end as easily as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) appears to think. I noted a recent public comment which was attributed to him to the effect that it would be a good way to celebrate July 1 by simply turning out the lights and lifting the controls.

Anyway, apparently he sees the whole program being suddenly dropped on June 30, that this would be a good idea, with the cabinet apparently arbitrarily dealing with the leftovers on the advice of a department that has the monitoring of salary and price increases suddenly added to its responsibilities simply as "other related duties".
I do not think it is a time for grandstanding, Mr. Speaker. I think it is a time for co-operation of the very highest order. I think that is as fundamental to the decontrol process as it has been during the life of the anti-inflation program.
As President of the Treasury Board representing in the government sense the employer, and having to apply the controls to our general expenditure restraint program, I can tell hon. members that we have had widespread and substantial support in making the restraint program work in what we call the bureaucratic system. Without that I do not think the progress that we have made could have been made, nor could it have been made so quickly. My cabinet colleagues and their departmental staffs certainly have not been happy from time to time at the many occasions when they have had to modify their submissions, but they have co-operated in an effort to trim government spending.
It has to be said in all fairness that the public service unions too have, with very few exceptions, tempered their demands in a way that underscores the observation in the green paper that inflationary expectations have decreased in Canada since 1975. This apparent change of attitudes and expectations by many segments of our society, coupled with our continuing commitment to keep inflation in check, bodes well for the immediate future.
In the area of fiscal matters I have already reminded members of my commitment, which has been stated several times, that the federal government will restrain its spending in line with relative growth in the gross national product. The record shows that in fiscal 1976-77 the GNP increased by 13.5 per cent and that our expenditure increase was held to 11 per cent.
June 17, 1977

During fiscal year 1977-78 the forecasters are looking for an 11 per cent increase in the gross national product. I have already told the House that we expect a federal expenditure increase over 1976 in the area of 7 per cent. That translates into a total expenditure for this fiscal year of $44,450 million, budgetary and non-budgetary, including all supplementary estimates through to March 31, 1978.
To emphasize the degree of restraint, that total figure of $44,450 million includes only $1,550 million reserve for all supplementary estimates for the whole of the fiscal year of which, by past experience, $850 million will probably be absorbed by unavoidable adjustments to existing programs, statutory and others. That will leave only $700 million for emergencies or new programs requiring new expenditures. Well, $700 million in absolute figures is a very, very sizeable amount. Relative to the total expenditures, however, it amounts to IV2 per cent. Relative to reserves after the main estimates within expenditure ceilings for any given year or relative to the cumulative supplementary estimates of previous years, that is very tight indeed. I doubt that any fortnight of debates in this House of Commons goes by without there being suggestions for spending from all sides in excess of that reserve.
1 have said that 1 did not get into politics to balance books or to be a bookkeeper, but in the face of the continuing need to combat inflation, and recognizing that the entire public sector-all governments in Canada-is now eating up more than 40 per cent of the GNP, up about 12 per cent from just over a decade ago, the bulk of which is at the provincial and municipal level, all of us in public office have got to maintain a determined effort and leave no stone unturned collectively in an attempt to keep our total public spending in line with the kind of commitments we have been making.

I make that statement with the full knowledge that emergencies and extraordinary situations may require extraordinary measures from time to time. However, our goal must be to keep federal spending growth in step with the GNP.
I heard the economist, Douglas Peters, comment the other day in Montreal at the CMA meeting. He suggested that we need major new incentives for manufacturing. I should like to ask him what he is willing to trade off in exchange. By the same token we, as members of parliament and politicians,
Anti-Inflation Act
must be prepared to cut back in established and existing programs if unavoidable new demands arise and have to be met. We cannot add new ideas requiring new expenditures on top of existing commitments without blowing the lid off.
I should like to comment for a few minutes on another important aspect which is very directly related to my portfolio, and that is the matter of public service compensation and collective bargaining. I do so in light of the anti-inflation program and the decontrol process.
At the outset I should like to state the obvious, and that is, we believe that collective bargaining is the fairest and most acceptable method of determining wages and working conditions for the federal public servant. We also believe in the principle of comparability of compensation wherever possible. It is very much more possible quantitatively than generally thought. I am referring to the comparability of compensation between the public servant and the employee in the private sector-between private industry and government.
There are those who feel that in this field of wage, salary and collective bargaining settlements that the federal government is a pacesetter, forcing wages and salaries up in the market place. The facts deny that allegation. Labour Canada provides a general picture by showing rates of increase in base wage rates for new settlements covering 500 employees. This is a matter of public information and public record. 1 should like to refer to that report which covers the period from 1968 to 1976. It excludes the construction industry.
That report indicates that for municipal public servants the base wage rate increase was 132 per cent; for provincial public servants that wage increase was 129 per cent; for the public sector as a whole the increase was 124 per cent; for all industries, both private and public, the increase was 123 per cent; for the private sector alone the increase was 120 per cent; and at the very bottom of the list the federal public servant wage increase was 113 per cent. Those numbers clearly indicate that the increase in base rates for federal public servants has been less than any other sector, including the private sector. It is equally clear that if the increases in the public sector as a whole are slightly higher than the average, that is due to increases at other than federal government levels.
I have read those statistics into the record because they set the stage for some of the information I would like to give hon. members now. It will add credence and emphasis to what I said at the outset-we are showing leadership during this period of the anti-inflation program.
The AIB summary of public service settlements submitted for review called for an average increase of lOVi per cent, which had been the first year guideline established by the regulations. In fact, just over 80 per cent of the compensation settlements or arbitral awards were at or under the guidelines. That should be compared to other settlements in other sectors of the economy. Outside the public service, the average increase submitted for review was slightly higher than the federal public service and nearly a full percentage point above the guidelines. Thus, even though the federal public service record of base rate increases since 1968 was the lowest on the

Anti-Inflation Act
list, it did not prevent us from meeting the same AIB guidelines which others apparently could not meet. And while I am told the anti-inflation program has not yet had a discernible impact on the number of strikes in the federal public service, I am heartened by the dramatic reversal in this kind of activity.
In 1974 one strike was recorded in the federal public service, involving 17,300 employees. The following year, 1975, there were 12 strikes, either illegal or legal, involving about 43,400 employees. And in 1976, the most recent year for which statistics are available, there were six strikes involving only 9,000 employees. During the same three-year period the number of workers involved in strikes in all sectors across Canada almost tripled to a high in 1976 of just under 1.6 million.
While the statistics I have quoted demonstrate the effectiveness of the AIB program, hon. members may wonder about its effect upon the employee. Did he suffer? Did he lose financial ground? Mr. Speaker, workers in this country have experienced a real annual increase in wage rates which, for some, was higher than in previous years. The federal public servant got a real increase of 4.9 per cent, the highest real gain for him since 1971, while in manufacturing average hourly earnings showed a real increase of 6.7 per cent, well above the real gain recorded in any of the previous five years.
So it is not a bad record. What this tells me is that even within the restraint program, even within the constraint of the guidelines, there was room for significant growth in real purchasing power for both the public servant and his counterpart in private industry.
In looking to the decontrol period, the government has already stated its belief that the process and timing for the ending of controls should be the same in both the public and the private sectors. We reject the recommendation which has come from some sources that arbitrary controls should continue to apply to public servants after they have been removed in the private sector. We feel that would be unfair and unworkable. Nevertheless, we feel improvements must be made in the system of public service compensation.
What we are talking about now, and have begun to discuss with the public service unions, is the idea that in the pursuit of the principle of average comparability with the private sector, collective bargaining in the public service must reflect total compensation. In other words, we must give full recognition to the value of wages, benefits and working conditions as part of the compensation package. In other words, we have to give full recognition not only to the wages paid but also to other benefits and working conditions when assessing the total compensation package. Having shown leadership in this area, we are in consultation with the provinces and we hope that they, too, will attempt to bargain on a similar basis of average comparability with the private sector taking total compensation into account.
Implementation of these policies requires the development of improved methods and more detailed data, along with continued consultation with bargaining agents, the pay research bureau and others. The Treasury Board is now in the process of developing detailed work plans which include provision for consultation with all interested parties; I am hopeful that these consultations, which will occur within the context of the green paper, will help clarify the approach to be taken in connection with the achievement of our compensation goals.
1 note that the other day the columnist, Maurice Western, writing in the Winnipeg Free Press, said that the controls program has very wide support and that it was the prospect of decontrols which had aroused apprehension. Well, Mr. Speaker, I outlined a few moments ago the way in which the Treasury Board proposes to proceed with regard to the public service. The green paper sets out the method by which we may proceed in relation to a wider spectrum. I guess that in the end the key word is co-operation. I do not think any one sector can do it alone. I also believe that, given this co-operation, there is no need for much of the apprehension which has been expressed.
I may say I am encouraged by various comments which have come to my attention such as statements made this week at the Canadian Gas Association meeting in Jasper which call into question some of the gloomy views expressed by hon. members opposite in this debate. At that meeting the President of the Conference Board of Canada is quoted as saying:
There is a new attitude developing in Canada today that the gloom and doom of the last few years has passed its peak.
I was encouraged, also, to hear of a comment at the same meeting by Mr. Stevens, who has just taken over as head of the Manufacturers Association of Canada. He said:
It appears that Canada is making the right economic and political decisions and will emerge from this period of adjustment as a stronger nation.
So in spite of the bombast and rhetoric of this debate there is support for the policies of the government, and I think it is a great deal more general than some of our critics in the last day or so would like to admit.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I welcome this opportunity to take part in this three-day debate brought about by the Conservative motion that the anti-inflation controls be ended at the end of June 1977. It is a privilege for me to bring my modest contribution to this debate which is very important for consumers and specially for those who are least able to defend themselves against inflationary pressures, such as the aged, the retired, the non-unionized wage-earners who receive only the minimum wage and others in similar circumstances.
It is difficult for me to understand why the opposition leader introduced such a motion at the present time when statistics show that the anti-inflation program, after 18 months of existence, has proven to be one of the most positive factors to check the price and wage increase rises we have experienced in the years 1974-75. What a strange attitude for the Progressive Conservatives to take by introducing this motion when a recent Gallup poll taken on May 4 last was showing that 70 per cent of Canadians support controls and 60 per cent of independent business concerns are against the removal of salary and price controls in 1977.
Mr. Speaker, it would be interesting to examine the attitude of the opposition these days, since it is neglecting an important legislative program now before the House to tackle a program which has already proved its efficiency and which has received the approval of the Canadian people. Does it want to divert public attention from recent Gallup polls on the popularity of political parties? Do they want us to forget the results of the recent by-elections? It could not be done better. Perhaps they want to forget the two last defections from their party, that is the members for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) and for Hochelaga (Mr. Lavoie) who have joined the Liberal party. Without trying to be clever, I could add that before long, other members of the Progressive Conservative Party in Quebec and elsewhere will join this side of the House or will leave political life. It is unfortunate that he is not here, but 1 noted yesterday the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) who was not very successful during the recent by-elections when he bit the dust. Fortunately the party held him back, because he too would have resigned-something he is well known for.
Anti-Inflation Act
Finally, there seem to be various reasons and since the motion must be discussed, let us consider the facts. The Canadian people must not think that the fight against inflation is over, according to Mr. Gerald Bouey, Governor of the Bank of Canada. In the 1976 annual report of the Bank of Canada released last March 21, Mr. Bouey expresses the opinion that 1976 must be considered as the first episode of Canada's fight to get rid of inflationary attitudes and behaviour and to restore the internal economic balance necessary to our future wealth. The report reminds us that the relatively high inflation rate of costs and prices continues to be very dangerous for the health of our economy.
Over the last years, the average nominal income increase of employed people was much higher than in the United States and too high compared to Canada's wealth. Mr. Bouey finds that Canada has become a high production cost country. As long as this situation lasts, he adds, we cannot hope to establish the solid foundations which are essential to the creation of jobs on which our future wealth will rely. On the other hand, the high rate of inflation has seriously affected our competitive position on international markets, which has been reflected in considerable deficits in our foreign trade. As a matter of fact, the average hourly wages for workers in the manufacturing sector of the economy, as of January 1976, were: Canada: $5.03; U.S.A.: $4.80; Sweden: $4.67; West Germany: $3.72; Japan: $3.13; Great Britain: $2.84; and France: $2.19.
Over the nearly one and a half year the anti-inflation program has been in effect, inflation has regressed in Canada. Although we could argue endlessly about the relative part played by the anti-inflation guidelines and other factors, such as the stagnation of the economy, on the control of price increases up to now, the fact remains that all relevant guidelines indicate that the pressures exerted by wage and price increases have been reduced. One year after the introduction of this program, that is, from October 1975 to October 1976, the rise in the consumer price index was 6.2 per cent, which is clearly lower than the 10.6 per cent for the year before. We were very much encouraged by these results when we compared them with the rise of 8 per cent in CPI which we had forecast for October 1976.
What matters more is the fact that the rate of price increases for goods other than food and energy has clearly started slowing down. However, the last CPI report indicates that prices had increased by 6.7 per cent in February compared with a year ago, for food prices had been greatly affected by adverse weather conditions in southern United States. The anti-inflation program objective for the second year, a 6 per cent increase in the CPI until October 1977, remains a challenge. In 1975, according to Labour Canada, wage settlements have averaged an annual increase of more than 20 per cent during their first year of implementation. During the four quarters of 1976, the increase rate has fallen respectively to 16, 12.8, 13.1 and 9.9 per cent. Because of an even lower rate of increase in the consumer price index, the net income increase for Canadians has kept on.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, 1 resume: -automatically approved by the AIB staff and the increases reflecting the decisions of the board as regard increases exceeding the directives. Those real increase rates, which started at an average of 13.4 per cent for cases settled before the program, then went down to 9.4 per cent during the first year of the program, and to 7 and 5.8 per cent for cases considered up to now during the second and third years of the program. As we are preparing to eliminate the controls and as we are getting closer to the 1980's, it is essential to assess our situation and our economic prospects.
As all other industrialized countries, Canada recently had to face the combined problems of inflation, unemployment and low growth. However we must not forget that Canadians did benefit from a significant increase, up to 5 per cent certain years, in their real per capita income. This increase was more rapid than that of any major accidental industrialized coun-

tries, and twice the average annual increase in the productivity per employee. That period witnessed a number of factors which were exceptionally favourable to Canada. First of all, while external influences added to our inflation problems, Canadians benefitted from a considerable improvement in the foreign exchange situation, the average price of their exports increasing much more rapidly than that of their imports. Secondly, Canada, over the whole period, was a major net exporter of energy, conditions being relatively favourable. Thirdly, thanks to a swifter increase in employment as compared with the population growth, and therefore a much higher proportion of Canadian families receiving two or three or even more pay cheques, the real income per capita increased significantly. Canada created employment for the major part of the labour force at an increasing rate, because of the considerable growth both in the population and the proportion of new workers.
Those favourable conditions could not last. There are limits to the amounts we can borrow abroad to sustain our present level of consumption. Since the international exchange profile is changing and developing countries keep on asking for a better distribution of the world wealth, we might have some problems to maintain favourable exchange conditions. Canada is definitively an importer of oil and in the short term may find itself in the same situation on the whole energy market. In order to realize our potential, we will have to adapt our economic structure. We should not expect too much from the economy either. Inflation is still a major impediment to the achievement of our collective and individual objectives.
Statistics show beyond any doubt that most Canadian workers are reasonably well off after the first year of the program. In spite of a definite slowdown, salaries and wages went up 10 per cent on average. At the same time, the consumer index increase was maintained below 6'A per cent. The unprecedented low level of food prices, the positive effect of prices of the Canadian currency which did resist during most of 1976 and margin benefits being exceptionally low due to the net decline in commercial activities in Canada and in the world, have allowed for a real increase in family income, salaries and wages of some 3'/2 to 4'/2 per cent, which is much above the 2 per cent of the labour productivity increase.
Mr. Speaker, the first duty of the government is to create an atmosphere which will enable private industry to develop in all confidence and to create lasting and satisfactory employment for workers. The present policy tries to establish this atmosphere. The government knows also that specific action is necessary in some areas and among certain categories because of unemployment rates. Therefore they changed their priorities in a federal policy providing for budgetary restrictions in an endeavour to increase support to direct employment programs.
There are signs in the present situation and in the economic prospects in Canada that the next twelve months or so should be a proper time for decontrol. First, given the present underuse of material and human resources in Canada, and in
June 17, 1977

industrialized nations in general, there is little danger of having a new inflationary explosion because of decontrol.
Second, although we cannot put aside the possibility of stock shortages, for instance because of generally poor crops, an oil embargo or a serious breakdown in the trade of a number of basic products, the general conditions of food, industrial raw materials and energy resources supply do not allow us to foresee any major shortage during the next two years. World prices for food, industrial raw materials and energy will probably go up, but at best at a slow pace. It is hardly likely, however, that these products, within the next two years, will be the cause of a price surge similar to that experienced recently.
What is more important is that the inflationary psychosis seems to have been going down considerably since October 1975. The man in the street no longer expects two-digit price or wage increases. Newspapers do not report any more astronomical wage increases which were an invitation to other workers to do the same. According to surveys among industries and consumers, no more rapid price hike is expected. The reduction of the spiral of expectations can be explained by the recent improvements in the control of prices, as well as by the government undertaking to avoid a major increase in the cost of living, through the anti-inflation program.
Therefore, there is a need for a decontrol process which will ensure a steady decrease in the inflation rates and contribute to restore confidence in the future of our economy. This means that we must assess our economic prospects on a realistic basis and take our share of responsibility in the Canadian economic performance. The government has considered the part it could play during the post-control period and set a number of principles to establish the future direction of federal policies. Here are some of these principles: the best way to achieve the Canadian economic potentialities is to ensure a more efficient market economy.
In line with society's expectations, the government is firmly committed to the safeguard of personal freedom, equal opportunities and social fairness. Social policy must protect and improve our evolutive society built up by Canadians without leading to continued government expansion and ongoing erosion of personal freedom.
Our national potential cannot be developed without healthy, dynamic regions. Confederation benefited all Canadians, because the advantages of a larger nation promoted the growth of each and every region. However, remaining regional disparities are a major challenge to our political institutions. Canadians cannot accept those disparities. Federal and provincial authorities have taken a number of significant initiatives. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion is supporting long-term development efforts by the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, in addition to providing a consultation forum, an organization that would monitor economic conditions in respect of their impact on prices and costs would make a major contribution to the improvement of our economic performance. This view is shared both by provincial governments, and certain groups in the private sector, as evidenced by preliminary consultations. In time, the supervising body could exert a
Anti-Inflation Act
significant, positive influence on prices and revenues, provided its organizational features and objectivity maintained the required level of credibility.
In ending controls, our foremost consideration should be to prevent soaring prices and incomes, which would signal a return to the previous situation. The tangible results of the controls program, namely a much less rapid increase in costs and prices, must absolutely be preserved and reinforced. Finally, the de-control plan must take place in an orderly fashion. An important area in which the public and private sectors both carry the responsibility of economic performance is labour and management relations. If, indeed, it is the government's role to define the legislative and institutional framework in which labour and management may bargain, both sides must ensure that the system is allowed to work. However, in the last few years the level of confidence in labour-management relationship has constantly deteriorated. The degree of acceptance by public opinion of the increased frequency of strikes and lockouts as well as the various inconveniences and costs that go along with these, is on the wane.
Mr. Speaker, the government expects to raise a public debate on these issues and get some feedback. The increasing uncertainty regarding the date set for de-controls has made it necessary to come to a decision as soon as possible. Therefore, one should consider the possibility of releasing the timing set for de-control by the middle of this coming summer. This decision would take into account the debate and the various reactions generated by this document. Without further delay, the issues at stake should become the subject of a public debate where various comments could be made. Consultations will take place with businesses, workers and other interest groups. The government will also consult the provinces to find out whether during that period it would be necessary to call a new federal-provincial conference of finance ministers. The government is counting on the general participation of Canadians in this debate and will try to devise some ways to achieve that. The government plans on holding a meeting to set a multipartite panel of discussion so as to further the debate on more precise matters, such as the nature of those future mechanisms of consultation and to debate on what the postcontrol period will be before taking a decision on the timing that will be chosen for de-control.
Once the process and the timing of the de-control plan will have been announced, it will be necessary to resume our studies on the various measures to be taken in the post-control era. We hope that the study of the various consultation mechanisms will be sufficiently advanced to allow those mechanisms to play an important part in the preparation of the decisions to be taken and as to the very precise shape that will have such institutions as the monitoring body and the consultation panel that have been proposed as well as the way they will work during the post-control period.
Mr. Speaker, contrary to the expressed views of the opposition, the Liberal government was not afraid through this difficult period in our economy to face up to its responsibilities and to adopt policies that will enable us to solve our problems.

June 17, 1977
Anti-Inflation Act
During the de-control and post-control period, we shall invite all Canadians to become involved in the shaping-up of the economic decisions upon which our progress will depend.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS OF JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is probably no surprise that this motion has come before the House at this time. The only surprise might be that, having 15 sitting days before it was necessary to debate it, the government scheduled the motion rather more quickly than we expected. Of course that was provided for in the bill which introduced the controls program.
It should also come as no surprise that it was the official opposition that presented the motion yesterday since only this party has consistently voted against the government's controls program. It is true there were other proposals for controls, but it is this party that consistently said a long-term program of controls would be ineffective in curbing inflation.
It was the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who said we had wrestled inflation to the ground, and we know what happened to inflation rates after he said that. It was the government and the Prime Minister who said controls per se would not work. It was the official opposition that in 1973 perceived the great concern of Canadians at the rate of inflation that the country was subjected to because of the government's programs. In 1974 it was the official opposition that campaigned honestly on a program of controls, pointing out to the Canadian people where the government was taking them with its profligate spending and lack of restraint.
History has shown that the people were not ready for the program of controls that the then Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) proposed. There were areas such as British Columbia, however, where people were willing to listen to the official opposition and take their medicine. They elected a majority of members to the House who explained why controls were necessary and why it was important for the government to take the responsible attitude on controls. But the Liberals said no. Then we had to wait for 14 months after the last election until changes began to manifest themselves.
While we cannot be sure, because it has never been said, we can ask ourselves where the former minister of finance and his leader differed on policy so greatly that the former minister was forced by his conscience to terminate not only his career as a minister but his career as a politician. We can blame him or we can blame the Prime Minister. Certainly we can blame the present government because it has had power in this country for too long. The Prime Minister has been in office for nine years, pulling the strings and trying to lay the blame on others because he has been unable to act.
It was the government that said in 1974 that controls would not work. It pointed to countries around the world and said controls did not work in the United States, the United Kingdom and a few other places. Just yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) said controls would be completely ineffective in controlling the price of imports. Certainly his

kind of controls would be, because they have been ineffective in controlling inflation.
The latest figures, published on the day the petition of the official opposition was filed, show that for 1977 inflation has been running at an annual rate of 10'/2 per cent. That is a little lower than it was earlier, but still a long way from control of inflation. If we had adopted a short-term freeze in 1974, as the official opposition proposed in order to break the inflationary expectations, then we could have controlled the prices of imports. Importers are businessmen and planners; they do not buy for tomorrow at today's prices. It would have been easy to control the price of imports with a three-month freeze.
It is now a fact that the controls program itself has become inflationary. No longer does labour begin to bargain around a rate of 15 per cent expecting to settle for something below 10 per cent. The floor of labour negotiations is now at least 8 per cent. In the controls legislation 8 per cent was only the base; it could have been 10 per cent in certain circumstances, and even 12 per cent if a historical relationship could be shown.
We never had a freeze so we never had an opportunity to find out what short-term controls would have done. All the government has shown us is that long-term controls have not controlled inflation and have not operated to the benefit of the Canadian economy.
I want to refer to an article which appeared in a recent issue of the magazine Business Week regarding the Canadian economy. I shall quote a paragraph or so. Referring to the Canadian dollar and the troubles of the Canadian economy, it says:
Inflation, averaging more than 9 per cent annually in the past four years and still running at a 7.5 per cent annual rate, has pushed Canadian costs above those of the U.S. and other industrial countries. As a result, Canadian products are being priced out of international markets, Canadians are crossing the border to shop in the U.S., and the nation's balance of payments is plunging deeply into deficit. . .
Business investment, meanwhile, is being discouraged by shrinking profits and worries among businessmen about future growth prospects. And business and labour unions alike are chafing under federal wage and price controls.
The article goes on to say that in 1972 Canada ran a trade deficit of $4.8 billion in manufactured goods, but by last year the deficit had more than doubled, to $10.2 billion.
What has happened under our controls program? Canada is no longer capable of attracting the investment of Canadians or the investment of foreigners. Many of us can point to instances of Canadians investing in the United States, particularly in housing. Perhaps one cannot blame the Minister of Finance on this score directly. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) complains about the lack of housing in Canada, but what does one find? One finds entrepreneurs, who would be willing in normal circumstances to provide housing for Canadians, taking their capital and expertise to the United States, there to build houses for Americans.
The article continues a little further along with these words:
Coiled around these problems-
June 17, 1977

Namely, the deficit and continued inflation.
-is a political crisis, the deepest in its 110 years of confederation, that is shaking the unity of Canada to its foundations. The ties that bind the 12 vast and disparate provinces and territories are being severely strained by Frenchspeaking Quebec's drive for greater political and cultural autonomy and by demands of other provinces, especially Alberta, for greater decentralization of decision making.
We can lay the blame for every one of these difficulties at the feet of the present administration, if not at the feet of the Prime Minister.
